description: Anamur Galaxy Crew, STEM/STEAM, bilim, teknoloji, tasarım ve yaratıcı problem çözmeyi bir araya getiren disiplinlerarası bir ekip. NASA’nın açık verilerini kullanarak Dünya ve uzayla ilgili gerçek problemlere yenilikçi çözümler geliştirmeyi hedefliyoruz. Yazılım, veri analizi, yapay zekâ, mühendislik, tasarım, uzay bilimleri, çevre, tarım ve hikâye anlatımı alanlarında ekip arkadaşları arıyoruz.

details:
AURA: Modular Mars Station & ISRU Ecosystem

Team Name: Anamur Space Team

Challenge: Mars & Deep Space Habitat Design / In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU)

Team Members: Zeynep Demir (Team Lead & Ecosystem Designer), Oğuz Demir (Modular Prototype Designer), Abdurrahman Çağdaş Demir (Visual Visionary & Mentor), Physics Mentor Mother (System & Energy Analyst)

1. Project Title & Executive Summary

Project Title: AURA: Modular Mars Station & ISRU Ecosystem

Executive Summary:

The primary constraint facing deep space missions is the astronomical cost of launching every single kilogram of material from Earth to Mars. Developed by Anamur Space Team, the AURA project utilizes In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) to melt and cut previously abandoned rocket bodies, heat shields, and landing hardware on Mars, transforming them into standardized interlocking "Lego-style" grid blocks.

Combining the family's multidisciplinary expertise—physics calculations, visual-architectural design, biomimicry, and a child's modular Lego perspective—the project constructs durable hangars from scrap metal while storing minerals from Martian regolith inside insulating biomimetic greenhouses inspired by silkworm cocoons. Anamur Space Team delivers a dynamic and sustainable architectural vision that transforms space debris into the habitats of tomorrow.

2. Problem Statement

  1. Astronomical Payload Cost: Launching 1 kg of structural payload from Earth to Mars costs over $100,000, severely limiting deep-space infrastructure development.
  2. Accumulated Space Debris: Spent Titanium and Aluminum-Lithium alloy rocket boosters, heat shields, and landing gear from previous exploration missions are left behind on the Martian surface as underutilized waste.

3. Technical & Architectural Solution

A. Space Debris Upcycling & Modular "Lego-Grid" System

  • In-Space Processing: Abandoned metallic hardware on the Martian surface is processed using mobile laser cutters and resharpening units, converting structural alloys into standardized "T-Slot" grid profiles and interlocking connectors.
  • Zero-Welding Assembly: Inspired by a 10-year-old child's Lego building logic, standardized interlocking joints allow astronauts to rapidly assemble launch pads, rover hangars, and habitat supports without importing additional welding materials from Earth.

B. Biomimetic Greenhouse & Mineral Storage

  • Inspired by Nature (Biomimicry): The habitat shell features a multi-layered geometry inspired by silkworm cocoons and desert lizard scales, engineered to withstand intense Martian dust storms and extreme temperature fluctuations.
  • Regolith Mineral Shielding: Minerals extracted from Martian soil (Iron, Magnesium, Silicon) are packed inside the outer matrix of the cocoon shell, acting as natural thermal insulation and a cosmic radiation shield.
  • Closed-Loop Life Support: The pressurized inner shell houses a vertical hydroponic farming system, supporting biological crop cultivation, water filtration, and atmospheric oxygen recycling for the crew.

C. Structural Physics & Functional Color Coding

  • Physical Modeling: Structural load tolerances and mass-energy loops are calculated for Mars’s surface gravity ($3.71 \, \text{m/s}^2$) and nighttime thermal retention.
  • Psychological Comfort: Functional color coding breaks the monotone red landscape of Mars, providing clear spatial navigation and psychological well-being for the mission crew.

4. NASA Open Data & Resources Used

  1. NASA ISRU Data Portal: Mars Regolith Composition, Mineral Extraction & Thermal Properties (data.nasa.gov)
  2. NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS): In-Space Manufacturing (ISM) & Metal Recycling Frameworks (ntrs.nasa.gov)
  3. NASA Planetary Data System (PDS): Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) Surface & Atmospheric Datasets (pds.nasa.gov)
  4. NASA Image & Video Library: Perseverance, Curiosity & Lander Hardware Archive (images.nasa.gov)
